newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's Mandela to take companion on Asia trip.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's Mandela to take companion on Asia trip.

text.p: South African President Nelson Mandela will show the world his new companion Graca Machel on Saturday when he begins an eight-day Asian visit, the first with her officially at his side.

A year after the bitter divorce from his second wife Winnie, Mandela will take Graca, the 51-year-old widow of former Mozambican president Samora Machel, as his official companion to the Philippines, Brunei, Singapore and Malaysia.

One of the world's most popular and charismatic leaders, he was accompanied by his daughter Zenani on his triumphant tour last July to Britain and France. Since he left Winnie in 1992, he has travelled with Zenani or grand-daughter Rochelle.
A presidential spokesman said neither Brunei nor Malaysia, the two Moslem countries Mandela, 78, will visit, had objected to him travelling with his unmarried companion.
"The president is not a Moslem. There is mutual respect between the countries," he said.
Trade will dominate the trip to a region that the new South Africa's leaders see as an economic model for their country.

Mandela will do more listening than preaching as he and a 30-strong business entourage try to fathom the economic success of the Asian "tigers" which South Africa would dearly like to emulate, political analysts said.

Malaysia became the fourth-biggest investor in South Africa last year, behind more traditional partners Britain, Germany and the United States, when the state oil firm Petronas bought 30 percent of listed South African company Engen Oil.
The former prisoner of apartheid South Africa will tour a Proton car plant, flagship of Malaysia's national-oriented economic policy.
"Malaysia's brand of state-steered nationalistic capitalism goes down well in Africa," wrote the specialist newsletter Africa Confidential.

It said Kuala Lumpur, with a determined Pretoria-centred Africa policy that has won it an influence extending beyond commerce, was instrumental in persuading Mandela last year to drop old ally Taiwan in favour of diplomatic ties with China.

Mandela's African National Congress has also held up Malaysia's bumiputera (sons of the land) strategy -- affirmative action for Malays in a country with a strong ethnic Chinese presence in business -- as a possible model for advancing South Africa's long-oppressed black majority.
In the Philippines, Mandela will visit Corazon Aquino, the former president whose "people's power" movement brought democracy to the country.
In Singapore Mandela, used to adulation from admiring crowds on his foreign tours, will have an orchid named after him in the National Orchid Gardens.
In Brunei, he and Graca will have a private dinner with His Majesty Sultan Haji Hassanal Bolkiah, one of the world's richest men.
The four-nation trip had originally been scheduled for last October but Mandela called it off at the last moment due to knee trouble.
